query: For high-entropy alloys intended for thermal-insulation or radiation-resistant applications, what single intervention could reduce phonon thermal conductivity? Formulate one testable hypothesis that specifies the intervention, the physical mechanism, the predicted change relative to an otherwise comparable untreated alloy, the temperature and material-state boundaries over which it should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment whose result would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing lattice distortion through alloying elements can reduce phonon thermal conductivity in high-entropy alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloy with a face-centered cubic (FCC) or body-centered cubic (BCC) structure
generation.intervention: Alloying with elements that introduce lattice distortion, such as tungsten or tantalum
generation.mechanism: Derived from materials-science principles, as lattice distortion and disorder can scatter phonons and reduce thermal conductivity
generation.predicted_outcome: Reduced phonon thermal conductivity by 10-20% compared to the untreated alloy
generation.baseline: Thermal conductivity of the untreated alloy
generation.boundary: Temperature range: 300-1000 K, Pressure: 1 atm, Alloy composition: High-entropy alloy with a face-centered cubic (FCC) or body-centered cubic (BCC) structure
generation.uncertainty: The exact reduction in thermal conductivity depends on the specific alloy composition and lattice distortion introduced

falsification_experiment.design: Measure thermal conductivity of the alloy with and without lattice distortion introduced by alloying elements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermal conductivity of the alloy with lattice distortion is not reduced by 10-20% compared to the untreated alloy, the hypothesis is falsified

A quinary WTaCrVHf nanocrystalline refractory high-entropy alloy withholding extreme irradiation environments

Abstract: AbstractIn the quest of new materials that can withstand severe irradiation and mechanical extremes for advanced applications (e.g. fission & fusion reactors, space applications, etc.), design, prediction and control of advanced materials beyond current material designs become paramount. Here, through a combined experimental and simulation methodology, we design a nanocrystalline refractory high entropy alloy (RHEA) system. Compositions assessed under extreme environments and in situ electron-microscopy reveal both high thermal stability and radiation resistance. We observe grain refinement under heavy ion irradiation and resistance to dual-beam irradiation and helium implantation in the form of low defect generation and evolution, as well as no detectable grain growth. The experimental and modeling results—showing a good agreement—can be applied to design and rapidly assess other alloys subjected to extreme environmental conditions.Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Power stations Refractory high entropy alloys (RHEAs) have recently been developed in the context

Phonon behavior in a random solid solution: a lattice dynamics study on the high-entropy alloy FeCoCrMnNi

Abstract: AbstractHigh-Entropy Alloys (HEAs) are a new family of crystalline random alloys with four or more elements in a simple unit cell, at the forefront of materials research for their exceptional mechanical properties. Their strong chemical disorder leads to mass and force-constant fluctuations which are expected to strongly reduce phonon lifetime, responsible for thermal transport, similarly to glasses. Still, the long range order would associate HEAs to crystals with a complex disordered unit cell. These two families of materials, however, exhibit very different phonon dynamics, still leading to similar thermal properties. The question arises on the positioning of HEAs in this context. Here we present an exhaustive experimental investigation of the lattice dynamics in a HEA, Fe20Co20Cr20Mn20Ni20, using inelastic neutron and X-ray scattering. We demonstrate that HEAs present unique phonon dynamics at the frontier between fully disordered and ordered materials, characterized by long-propagating acoustic phonons in the whole Brillouin zone.Subject terms: Electronic proper
